claims.text: The initial catalyst is a nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
Durability during ethanol oxidation is governed by reversible oxidation-reduction cycling of surface metal sites, especially Os and Ir.
Extended anodic holds drive oxidation of surface metal sites.
Os and Ir are the surface sites particularly susceptible to oxidation under the proposed protocol.
Anodic treatment dynamically changes the oxidation state and coordination environment of the catalyst surface.
The proposed surface oxidation and coordination changes can be monitored by in situ XANES/EXAFS.
Oxidized surface sites form oxide or hydroxide species.
Surface oxide or hydroxide species modify the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Moderate surface oxidation is reversible and improves durability by tuning intermediate binding.
Oxidation beyond a threshold causes irreversible degradation and reduces catalyst longevity.
Relative to short anodic holds, extended holds will produce a larger oxidized fraction of Os and Ir.
Extended anodic holds will initially cause a transient stabilization or enhancement of catalytic activity.
Sufficiently long anodic holds will eventually cause a noticeable decline in activity and durability.
Short anodic holds minimize significant surface oxidation and provide an appropriate baseline.
The proposed test compares short and extended anodic holds while concurrently measuring oxidation state and electrochemical performance.
The hypothesis is scoped to ethanol oxidation in 0.5 M sulfuric acid at room temperature over 0.2–1.0 V versus RHE.
Physical restructuring, sintering, mass loss, or irreversible dissolution could independently contribute to performance loss.
Failure of oxidation-state cycling to correlate systematically with activity or durability would falsify the proposed mechanism.
